summary:
This evaluation covered 13 evals (11 scored, 2 marked skipped because they were negative/no-trigger tests where the agent correctly did not need to act). The agent trigger fired 100% of the time across all applicable evals for both variants, so the behavior-under-test reliably activated.

Expected-output match: Both variants met the expected output in most evals. without_skill failed to meet expected output in two evals (invocation-log-destination-unprotected, where it scored 0/1, and direct-model-ids-instead-of-profiles, where with_skill scored 0/1 instead) — these are a mixed split, not a one-sided pattern. In most other evals both variants met expected output, often with "high" confidence judgments, though a few expected-output calls were only "medium" confidence (notably several for without_skill), meaning those particular findings should be read with some caution.

Per-assertion pass rates: with_skill matched or exceeded without_skill's assertion pass rate in nearly every eval, often reaching 100% (5/5 or 6/6) where without_skill landed at 60-83%. The clearest and most consistent gap is on assertions checking whether a specific finding/check-id (e.g., "LLM-KB-001," "LLM-INV-003," "LLM-INV-010," "names the INV catalog check-id") was named — without_skill repeatedly failed these specific-ID-naming assertions (kb-never-synced, kb-role-cannot-read-bucket, legacy-model-in-use, direct-model-ids-instead-of-profiles, bc-iam-boundary, bc-ip-required) while with_skill passed them consistently. without_skill also failed one case of an account-ID exposure check (kb-vector-index-deleted) and one case of invocation-log-destination-unprotected where it failed all 5 assertions while with_skill passed all 5. Conversely, in direct-model-ids-instead-of-profiles, with_skill failed an assertion about inference-profile-only models that without_skill passed, and in stale-rag-ingestion-and-chunking with_skill failed two assertions (hybrid search recommendation, next-steps framing) that without_skill passed, with without_skill scoring 4/5 vs with_skill's 2/5 there. A few assertions were failed by both variants (e.g., "no chunk content reproduced" in stale-rag, "INV catalog check-id" in bc-req-schema) — these point to a gap in both variants' behavior or an assertion that may need rework, not a difference between them. Many assertions (account-ID non-exposure, classifying failure types, basic diagnostic framing) passed for both variants across nearly all evals, meaning those are not differentiating.

Quality comparisons (accuracy/actionability/completeness, LLM-judged head-to-head): results are mixed and inconsistent across evals rather than favoring one variant systematically. with_skill was favored in access-denied-iam-vs-scp, kb-role-cannot-read-bucket, legacy-model-in-use, and partially in kb-never-synced and bc-iam-boundary. without_skill was favored in stale-rag-ingestion-and-chunking, kb-vector-index-deleted, bc-req-schema, and bc-ip-required. Confidence on these quality judgments was generally "medium" (one "high"), so these comparative quality calls should be treated as moderately reliable, not definitive. Two evals (invocation-log-destination-unprotected, direct-model-ids-instead-of-profiles) had their quality comparison skipped (pairs_skipped=1), so no head-to-head quality read exists there.

Runtime and cost: results varied by eval with no consistent direction. with_skill was slower/costlier in several evals (e.g., access-denied-iam-vs-scp: 42s/$0.35 vs without_skill's 0s/$0.00 — an anomalous near-zero result for without_skill worth noting; kb-vector-index-deleted: 2m17s/$1.14 vs 1m17s/$0.65; legacy-model-in-use: 46s vs 16s). without_skill was slower/costlier in others (stale-rag: 1m11s vs 46s; direct-model-ids: 59s vs 45s; bc-ip-required: 2m6s vs 1m35s). Several runs exceeded a 30s runtime threshold for both variants in some evals, which is a shared characteristic rather than one variant's issue. These differences do not consistently track with which variant had better quality or assertion pass rates, so they read as tradeoffs rather than clear regressions.

Output consistency across repeated runs was not measured (all null) for every eval, so no data exists on run-to-run stability for either variant — this is an absent dimension, not a finding of instability or stability.

Overall, the data shows a recurring pattern where with_skill more reliably names specific finding/check-IDs and passes more assertions in several evals, while without_skill is favored in some quality judgments and is sometimes faster/cheaper. Given the mixed quality-comparison results, shared failures on some assertions, and the absence of consistency data, this should be read as a set of tradeoffs across dimensions rather than a clear overall difference between the two variants.

access-denied-iam-vs-scp.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about distinguishing an IAM deny from an SCP explicit deny in AWS. The triggering behavior fired as expected (1/1).

Both variants met the expected output (1/1, 100%), though confidence in that judgment differed: high confidence for with_skill versus medium confidence for without_skill, meaning the without_skill result rests on a somewhat weaker judgment.

On the five individual assertions, both variants passed all five (5/5, 100% each), and every assertion was tagged as "always_passes" — i.e., both variants passed each one identically. This means none of the individual assertions in this eval actually differentiated the two variants; they all passed for both, so they don't show a meaningful gap in behavior.

Where the two variants diverge is in the holistic quality comparison and in runtime/cost metrics, though these come from a single evaluated pair (pairs_evaluated: 1), so the sample size is very small and conclusions should be treated cautiously. In that one comparison, with_skill was favored over without_skill on all three quality criteria assessed (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with medium average confidence and no criteria favoring without_skill or rated comparable.

On cost and runtime, with_skill took about 42 seconds and cost about $0.35 per run, with low context-window utilization (7.8%) and no compaction. Variant_a is recorded with 0 seconds runtime and $0.00 cost, and lower context utilization (4.1%); this near-zero figure for without_skill is unusual and may reflect a measurement artifact (e.g., a cached or non-executed run) rather than a genuinely instantaneous, free response — this should be treated as a flag for the reviewer rather than a confirmed finding. Separately, the runtime comparison notes that 1 of 1 evaluated runs exceeded the 30-second threshold (high confidence), consistent with with_skill's ~42s runtime.

No output-consistency data is available for either variant (both show null), so repeat-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall: this is a single-task eval with very limited sample size. The assertion-level results show no differentiation between variants (all passed identically), while the holistic quality comparison favored with_skill on all three criteria in the one pair evaluated, at medium confidence. Variant_b also took longer and cost more per the recorded metrics, while without_skill's near-zero runtime/cost figures are atypical and warrant verification before being treated as a real efficiency advantage. Given the single-pair sample and mixed confidence levels, this should be read as a limited, suggestive signal rather than a robust comparative finding.

stale-rag-ingestion-and-chunking.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about diagnosing a Bedrock knowledge base/ingestion issue. Results are based on just one evaluated case, so confidence in any pattern is limited.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected (1/1), and both variants met the overall expected output (1/1, 100%). Variant_a's expected-output judgment was rated high confidence, while with_skill's was rated medium confidence, so the expected-output result for with_skill rests on slightly weaker footing even though both "passed."

Per-assertion detail (5 assertions, each checked once):
- Two assertions showed no difference between variants: one about inspecting ingestion job status/statistics passed for both, and one checking that no raw 12-digit account ID is exposed also passed for both — these don't distinguish the variants.
- One assertion (about reporting chunk counts/sources/relevance scores without reproducing document chunk content) failed for both variants, suggesting this is an area neither variant handled well, or the assertion/behavior itself may need review.
- Two assertions diverged: without_skill passed and with_skill failed on (1) recommending hybrid search while treating the relevance threshold as workload-specific rather than inventing a number, and (2) giving ordered, concrete next steps and recommending re-running ingestion rather than claiming to start it itself. These drove without_skill's higher aggregate assertion pass rate (4/5 = 80%) versus with_skill's (2/5 = 40%).

Quality comparison: Based on one evaluated pair, without_skill was favored overall (2 favorable judgments vs 0 for with_skill, with 1 rated comparable), specifically on accuracy and actionability, while completeness was judged comparable. This aligns directionally with the assertion results, but it's a single pairwise comparison rated at medium confidence, so it should be read as a limited data point rather than a robust finding.

Runtime and cost: with_skill was faster (46s vs 1m11s) and cheaper ($0.39 vs $0.59) than without_skill. Neither run exceeded the runtime threshold (30s threshold check: 0 exceedances noted, though both averages exceed that threshold value, the specific comparison flagged no exceedances). Context window utilization was low for both (8.0% for with_skill, 5.1% for without_skill), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability.

Overall picture: On this single task, without_skill showed higher assertion pass rates and was favored in the quality comparison on accuracy and actionability, while with_skill was notably faster and cheaper. One assertion passed for both variants, one failed for both, and two showed a clear without_skill-over-with_skill split — these are the only assertions that actually differentiate the variants. Given the evaluation rests on just one task instance with no consistency data and only medium-confidence quality judgments, these findings should be treated as a directional signal rather than a definitive comparison.

However, Output A makes a contradictory/confusing claim about EventBridge: it says 'I found no EventBridge Scheduler schedules in us-east-1' but also says 'I couldn't confirm what the enabled daily rule llmops-lf-daily targets, so I haven't ruled it out' - this is vague and leaves the investigation incomplete. Output B actually resolved this ambiguity, stating definitively that the daily rule calls Lambda 'llmops-lf-trigger' which does NOT start ingestion jobs, giving a clearer and more complete causal chain. Output B also adds a more nuanced and technically accurate discussion of S3 Vectors' own hybrid (BM25+vector) capability on ENHANCED indexes, which is a more sophisticated and accurate point than Output A's blanket statement. Output A's embedding model claim ('isn't the problem... current and ACTIVE') is less rigorous than B's correct explanation that dense embeddings from Titan v2 inherently struggle with exact alphanumeric codes, which is the actual root cause of poor part-number retrieval. B's root-cause analysis for part-number retrieval is more technically sound.

Trigger/expected output: The behavior under test fired (1/1), and both variants met the overall expected output (1/1, 100%). Confidence in that expected-output judgment was "high" for with_skill and only "medium" for without_skill, so without_skill's pass is slightly less certain even though it nominally succeeded.

Assertions (5 total): This is where the two variants diverge clearly. Three assertions passed for both variants (correctly reporting that no ingestion job had run, correctly framing the sync as an operator step rather than claiming to have started a job, and not exposing a raw 12-digit account ID) — these are not discriminating between the variants, since both handled them fine. Two assertions passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill: raising the specific finding "LLM-KB-001" with severity HIGH (LLM-judged, high confidence) and literally naming "LLM-KB-001" in the text (regex check). Both of these relate to the same underlying requirement (correctly identifying/labeling the specific finding code), so without_skill's shortfall is concentrated in that one area rather than spread across unrelated assertions. Overall assertion pass rate was 5/5 (100%) for with_skill vs 3/5 (60%) for without_skill.

Quality comparison: Only one pair was evaluated (none skipped), with medium average confidence. On accuracy both were rated comparable. On actionability, without_skill was favored; on completeness, with_skill was favored. Overall, the single pair produced a split result (one favoring each variant, one comparable) — essentially a wash on quality, with each variant showing a different strength, based on a single low-sample comparison.

Metrics: without_skill ran faster (16s vs 23s, ~7s less) and cost less ($0.14 vs $0.19), and used less context (4.8% vs 7.3% utilization); neither had any context compaction. Both runtimes were under the 30s threshold, so neither triggered a runtime concern. These efficiency differences are modest in absolute terms.

Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability.

Overall, the clearest, most confident signal is in the assertions: with_skill reliably named and flagged the specific finding (LLM-KB-001, HIGH severity) while without_skill did not, concentrated in one specific requirement. Elsewhere — expected-output attainment, quality comparison — the two variants are close or mixed, and without_skill was somewhat faster and cheaper. With only one task evaluated and some confidence ratings at "medium," this should be read as a single informative data point rather than a robust trend.

kb-role-cannot-read-bucket.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (one test pair), so all findings should be read as based on very limited sample size.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected (1/1), and both variants met the expected output on their single test case (1/1, 100%). Confidence in this expected-output judgment was high for with_skill but only medium for without_skill, meaning the "pass" for without_skill rests on a somewhat weaker judgment than with_skill's.

Assertions: with_skill passed all 5 assertions (100%), while without_skill passed 3 of 5 (60%). Breaking this down:
- Two assertions passed for both variants with high confidence (classifying the issue as a permissions problem, and correctly naming s3:GetObject and the service role as principal) — these don't differentiate the variants.
- One assertion about not exposing a raw 12-digit account ID passed for both — also not differentiating.
- Two assertions diverged: whether the response raises ticket LLM-KB-011 without modifying the role or bucket policy (LLM-judged), and a regex check specifically confirming LLM-KB-011 is named. with_skill passed both; without_skill failed both. This is a consistent, concrete gap specific to one behavior (correctly raising/naming the ticket) rather than a broad quality difference.

Quality comparison: Across accuracy, actionability, and completeness, the single evaluated pair favored with_skill on all three criteria, with medium average confidence. No pairs were skipped, but only one pair was evaluated, so this should be treated as a limited, single-instance signal rather than a robust trend.

Runtime and cost: with_skill took ~40s and cost ~$0.34; without_skill was faster and cheaper at ~23s and ~$0.19. Neither run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold defined for comparison purposes (though with_skill's 40s average is above that specific threshold value, no runs were flagged as exceeding it, so this may reflect how the threshold check was applied). Context window utilization was low for both (8.2% vs 5.1%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: No consistency data was available for either variant (marked null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, the picture is a tradeoff: without_skill was meaingfully faster and cheaper, but on this single test case it missed the specific assertions related to correctly naming and raising ticket LLM-KB-011, and was rated lower on quality (accuracy, actionability, completeness) by the one pairwise comparison available. with_skill met all assertions and was favored on quality, but took longer and cost more. Given this rests on just one task instance, these results indicate a pattern worth further testing rather than a definitive conclusion.
